tools.name: configuration_view
tools.description: Get the current Kubernetes configuration content as a kubeconfig YAML

minified.description: Return a minified version of the configuration. If set to true, keeps only the current-context and the relevant pieces of the configuration for that context. If set to false, all contexts, clusters, auth-infos, and users are returned in the configuration. (Optional, default true)

tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: helm_install
tools.description: Install (deploy) a Helm chart to create a release in the current or provided namespace

chart.description: Chart reference to install (for example: stable/grafana, oci://ghcr.io/nginxinc/charts/nginx-ingress)

name.description: Name of the Helm release (Optional, random name if not provided)

namespace.description: Namespace to install the Helm chart in (Optional, current namespace if not provided)

values.description: Values to pass to the Helm chart (Optional)

tools.name: helm_list
tools.description: List all the Helm releases in the current or provided namespace (or in all namespaces if specified)

all_namespaces.description: If true, lists all Helm releases in all namespaces ignoring the namespace argument (Optional)

namespace.description: Namespace to list Helm releases from (Optional, all namespaces if not provided)

tools.name: helm_uninstall
tools.description: Uninstall a Helm release in the current or provided namespace

name.description: Name of the Helm release to uninstall

namespace.description: Namespace to uninstall the Helm release from (Optional, current namespace if not provided)

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Provides comprehensive metrics including CPU, memory, filesystem, and network usage at the node, pod, and container levels. On systems with cgroup v2 and kernel 4.20+, also includes PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics that show resource pressure for CPU, memory, and I/O. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/ for details on PSI metrics

name.description: Name of the node to get stats from

tools.name: nodes_top
tools.description: List the resource consumption (CPU and memory) as recorded by the Kubernetes Metrics Server for the specified Kubernetes Nodes or all nodes in the cluster

label_selector.description: Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'node-role.kubernetes.io/worker=') to filter nodes by label (Optional, only applicable when name is not provided)

name.description: Name of the Node to get the resource consumption from (Optional, all Nodes if not provided)

Done. Here’s what I set up in canary-deployment-ns:

- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - replicas: 2
  - labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - container name/port/security config match the stable deployment (containerPort 80; no extra securityContext added)
- Updated Service recommendation-engine to select app=recommendation-engine (removed the version=v2.0 constraint) so it targets both deployments. Port config unchanged (port 80 -> targetPort 8080), matching your current setup.

Result
- With engine-v2-0 (2 pods) and engine-v2-1 (2 pods) behind the same Service, traffic will be roughly 50/50 across all 4 pods.
- Current pods:
  - engine-v2-0-d99685f59-9j5kr (v2.0) Running
  - engine-v2-0-d99685f59-rtj2g (v2.0) Running
  - engine-v2-1-7994887c57-7jk8p (v2.1) Running
  - engine-v2-1-7994887c57-9d564 (v2.1) Running

Verification tips
- Check endpoints: kubectl get endpoints -n canary-deployment-ns recommendation-engine -o wide (you should see 4 pod IPs).
- Check pod distribution: kubectl get pods -n canary-deployment-ns -l app=recommendation-engine -o wide

Adjust/rollback
- To send 100% traffic back to stable: update the Service selector to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.
- To change the canary weight: scale engine-v2-1 up/down to alter the pod ratio.
- To remove the canary: delete the engine-v2-1 Deployment.

Note: Service-level balancing is approximate. For precise weighted routing, you’d need an Ingress/controller or service mesh that supports traffic splitting.

Steps.message:
namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done. Here’s what I set up in canary-deployment-ns:

- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - replicas: 2
  - labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - container name/port/security config match the stable deployment (containerPort 80; no extra securityContext added)
- Updated Service recommendation-engine to select app=recommendation-engine (removed the version=v2.0 constraint) so it targets both deployments. Port config unchanged (port 80 -> targetPort 8080), matching your current setup.

Result
- With engine-v2-0 (2 pods) and engine-v2-1 (2 pods) behind the same Service, traffic will be roughly 50/50 across all 4 pods.
- Current pods:
  - engine-v2-0-d99685f59-9j5kr (v2.0) Running
  - engine-v2-0-d99685f59-rtj2g (v2.0) Running
  - engine-v2-1-7994887c57-7jk8p (v2.1) Running
  - engine-v2-1-7994887c57-9d564 (v2.1) Running

Verification tips
- Check endpoints: kubectl get endpoints -n canary-deployment-ns recommendation-engine -o wide (you should see 4 pod IPs).
- Check pod distribution: kubectl get pods -n canary-deployment-ns -l app=recommendation-engine -o wide

Adjust/rollback
- To send 100% traffic back to stable: update the Service selector to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.
- To change the canary weight: scale engine-v2-1 up/down to alter the pod ratio.
- To remove the canary: delete the engine-v2-1 Deployment.

Note: Service-level balancing is approximate. For precise weighted routing, you’d need an Ingress/controller or service mesh that supports traffic splitting.

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Deployment overrode the container command to run: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, which does not exist, causing a CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed
- Recreated the app Deployment without the custom command/args so the nginx-unprivileged image uses its default startup.
- Set imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent and exposed containerPort 8080 (the default port for nginx-unprivileged).

Current state
- Pod app-c88f5d4bc-vlmcf is Running (1/1) in crashloop-test.
- Recent events no longer show BackOff.

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Deployment overrode the container command to run: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, which does not exist, causing a CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed
- Recreated the app Deployment without the custom command/args so the nginx-unprivileged image uses its default startup.
- Set imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent and exposed containerPort 8080 (the default port for nginx-unprivileged).

Current state
- Pod app-c88f5d4bc-vlmcf is Running (1/1) in crashloop-test.
- Recent events no longer show BackOff.

Want me to also create a Service to expose this on a ClusterIP or NodePort, or add a readiness/liveness probe?

results.taskOutput:
I found the Deployment failing due to an invalid container image tag and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Pod was in ImagePullBackOff: image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag does not exist (ErrImagePull, NotFound).

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment’s container image to nginx:stable-alpine.
- I first tried quay.io/nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:stable-alpine, but the registry returned 401 Unauthorized in this cluster, so I switched to the official nginx image from Docker Hub.

Current status
- Deployment debug/app is healthy and Available.
- Replicas: 1 desired / 1 updated / 1 available.
- Current image: nginx:stable-alpine.
- Example running Pod: app-8bd585d66-qvrdh (1/1 Running).

Optional next steps
- If you prefer the nginxinc unprivileged image from Quay, provide imagePullSecrets (or ensure public access), and I can switch it over.
- Would you like me to pin the image to a specific version or digest for reproducibility?

outputSteps.content:
I found the Deployment failing due to an invalid container image tag and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Pod was in ImagePullBackOff: image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag does not exist (ErrImagePull, NotFound).

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment’s container image to nginx:stable-alpine.
- I first tried quay.io/nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:stable-alpine, but the registry returned 401 Unauthorized in this cluster, so I switched to the official nginx image from Docker Hub.

Current status
- Deployment debug/app is healthy and Available.
- Replicas: 1 desired / 1 updated / 1 available.
- Current image: nginx:stable-alpine.
- Example running Pod: app-8bd585d66-qvrdh (1/1 Running).

Optional next steps
- If you prefer the nginxinc unprivileged image from Quay, provide imagePullSecrets (or ensure public access), and I can switch it over.
- Would you like me to pin the image to a specific version or digest for reproducibility?

results.taskOutput:
Fixed.

- Root cause: The pod mounts PVC homepage-pvc, which requested storageClassName: sc. That StorageClass didn’t exist, so the PVC stayed Pending and the pod was Unschedulable.
- What I did: Created a StorageClass named sc using the Minikube hostpath provisioner (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath).
- Result:
  - PVC homepage-pvc is now Bound (1Gi).
  - Pod homepage-pod is Running and Ready (1/1) on node mcp-eval-cluster.

If you intended to use a different StorageClass (e.g., “standard” or “csi-hostpath-sc”), tell me and I can re-provision the PVC with the desired class and migrate the data.

namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created

Fixed.

- Root cause: The pod mounts PVC homepage-pvc, which requested storageClassName: sc. That StorageClass didn’t exist, so the PVC stayed Pending and the pod was Unschedulable.
- What I did: Created a StorageClass named sc using the Minikube hostpath provisioner (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath).
- Result:
  - PVC homepage-pvc is now Bound (1Gi).
  - Pod homepage-pod is Running and Ready (1/1) on node mcp-eval-cluster.

If you intended to use a different StorageClass (e.g., “standard” or “csi-hostpath-sc”), tell me and I can re-provision the PVC with the desired class and migrate the data.

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

- Root cause: The pod mounts PVC homepage-pvc, which requested storageClassName: sc. That StorageClass didn’t exist, so the PVC stayed Pending and the pod was Unschedulable.
- What I did: Created a StorageClass named sc using the Minikube hostpath provisioner (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath).
- Result:
  - PVC homepage-pvc is now Bound (1Gi).
  - Pod homepage-pod is Running and Ready (1/1) on node mcp-eval-cluster.

If you intended to use a different StorageClass (e.g., “standard” or “csi-hostpath-sc”), tell me and I can re-provision the PVC with the desired class and migrate the data.

I investigated and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Pod was “Running” but not Ready. Events showed liveness/readiness probes failing on http://:80/get_status and /is_ready with connection refused.
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80) and doesn’t expose those custom paths.

What I changed
- Deployment: updated health checks to GET / on port 8080 and exposed container port 8080.
- Service: kept service port at 80 but changed targetPort to 8080 so clients can still use port 80.

Current status
- Pod: webapp is 1/1 Ready and Running.
- Service: webapp points to the healthy Pod.

How to verify quickly
- kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
- curl http://localhost:8080  (should return the NGINX welcome page)

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the pods:
  - Service web/nginx had selector app=web.
  - The Deployment and pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: Endpoints for the Service were empty, so no traffic could reach any pod.
- Port mismatch:
  - The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80).
  - The Service targetPort was 80, so even after fixing the selector, traffic would still fail.

What I changed (now fixed)
- Updated the Service selector to match the pods (app=nginx).
- Updated the Service targetPort to 8080 to match the container’s listening port.

Current Service (key fields)
- type: ClusterIP
- selector: app: nginx
- ports:
  - port: 80
  - targetPort: 8080

Validation performed
- Endpoints now show the backing pod and correct port: 10.244.0.27:8080.
- Launched a temporary netshoot pod and curled http://nginx inside the cluster; received HTTP/1.1 200 OK with the default nginx page.
- Cleaned up the temporary test pods.

Notes and next steps
- The Service is ClusterIP, which is only accessible inside the cluster. If you need external access, choose one:
  - Expose as NodePort (simple, opens a high port on each node).
  - Use a LoadBalancer Service (if your cluster supports it).
  - Create an Ingress with an ingress controller.

If you want, I can expose it externally and set up either NodePort, LoadBalancer, or an Ingress for you.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the pods:
  - Service web/nginx had selector app=web.
  - The Deployment and pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: Endpoints for the Service were empty, so no traffic could reach any pod.
- Port mismatch:
  - The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80).
  - The Service targetPort was 80, so even after fixing the selector, traffic would still fail.

What I changed (now fixed)
- Updated the Service selector to match the pods (app=nginx).
- Updated the Service targetPort to 8080 to match the container’s listening port.

Current Service (key fields)
- type: ClusterIP
- selector: app: nginx

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the pods:
  - Service web/nginx had selector app=web.
  - The Deployment and pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: Endpoints for the Service were empty, so no traffic could reach any pod.
- Port mismatch:
  - The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80).
  - The Service targetPort was 80, so even after fixing the selector, traffic would still fail.

What I changed (now fixed)
- Updated the Service selector to match the pods (app=nginx).
- Updated the Service targetPort to 8080 to match the container’s listening port.

Current Service (key fields)
- type: ClusterIP
- selector: app: nginx
- ports:
  - port: 80
  - targetPort: 8080

Validation performed
- Endpoints now show the backing pod and correct port: 10.244.0.27:8080.
- Launched a temporary netshoot pod and curled http://nginx inside the cluster; received HTTP/1.1 200 OK with the default nginx page.
- Cleaned up the temporary test pods.

Notes and next steps
- The Service is ClusterIP, which is only accessible inside the cluster. If you need external access, choose one:
  - Expose as NodePort (simple, opens a high port on each node).
  - Use a LoadBalancer Service (if your cluster supports it).
  - Create an Ingress with an ingress controller.

If you want, I can expose it externally and set up either NodePort, LoadBalancer, or an Ingress for you.

results.taskOutput:
Summary of what I found
- Root cause: The web-app pods were stuck Pending due to an overly restrictive nodeSelector on the Deployment:
  nodeSelector: { environment: production-gpu }
  Your cluster’s only node does not have this label, so the scheduler couldn’t place any pods. As a result, the Service had no endpoints, leading to connection refused.
- Evidence:
  - Events showed FailedScheduling: "didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector."
  - Nodes have no environment=production-gpu label.
  - EndpointSlice initially had no endpoints; after the fix it shows endpoints.

What I changed to fix it
- Removed the nodeSelector from the webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment so pods can schedule on available nodes.

Current state
- Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment is Available with 2/2 pods Running.
- Service webshop-frontend/web-app-service now has 2 endpoints (e.g., 10.244.0.32, 10.244.0.33).
- This should resolve the connection refused errors from the frontend, since the service now routes to healthy pods.

How you can validate
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get deploy,po,svc
  - Expect the deployment to be Available and both pods Running.
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpointslices.discovery.k8s.io web-app-service-*
  - Expect two IPs listed under endpoints.
- Optional in-cluster check:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run tmp-curl --rm -it --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.6.0 -- curl -sI http://web-app-service
    - Expect HTTP/1.1 200 OK from nginx.

Notes to prevent recurrence
- If you truly need to target specific nodes, either:
  - Label the intended nodes (e.g., kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu), or
  - Use nodeAffinity with a preferred (soft) rule instead of a hard nodeSelector, so the app can still schedule if the labeled nodes aren’t available.
- Keep Service selectors aligned with pod labels (they are correct here: app=web-app).

I also cleaned up the short-lived test pods I created. Let me know if you want me to reintroduce a safer scheduling rule (e.g., preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution) or add node labels to match your intended topology.

Summary of what I found
- Root cause: The web-app pods were stuck Pending due to an overly restrictive nodeSelector on the Deployment:
  nodeSelector: { environment: production-gpu }
  Your cluster’s only node does not have this label, so the scheduler couldn’t place any pods. As a result, the Service had no endpoints, leading to connection refused.
- Evidence:
  - Events showed FailedScheduling: "didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector."
  - Nodes have no environment=production-gpu label.
  - EndpointSlice initially had no endpoints; after the fix it shows endpoints.

What I changed to fix it

outputSteps.content:
Summary of what I found
- Root cause: The web-app pods were stuck Pending due to an overly restrictive nodeSelector on the Deployment:
  nodeSelector: { environment: production-gpu }
  Your cluster’s only node does not have this label, so the scheduler couldn’t place any pods. As a result, the Service had no endpoints, leading to connection refused.
- Evidence:
  - Events showed FailedScheduling: "didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector."
  - Nodes have no environment=production-gpu label.
  - EndpointSlice initially had no endpoints; after the fix it shows endpoints.

What I changed to fix it
- Removed the nodeSelector from the webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment so pods can schedule on available nodes.

Current state
- Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment is Available with 2/2 pods Running.
- Service webshop-frontend/web-app-service now has 2 endpoints (e.g., 10.244.0.32, 10.244.0.33).
- This should resolve the connection refused errors from the frontend, since the service now routes to healthy pods.

How you can validate
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get deploy,po,svc
  - Expect the deployment to be Available and both pods Running.
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpointslices.discovery.k8s.io web-app-service-*
  - Expect two IPs listed under endpoints.
- Optional in-cluster check:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run tmp-curl --rm -it --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.6.0 -- curl -sI http://web-app-service
    - Expect HTTP/1.1 200 OK from nginx.

Notes to prevent recurrence
- If you truly need to target specific nodes, either:
  - Label the intended nodes (e.g., kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu), or
  - Use nodeAffinity with a preferred (soft) rule instead of a hard nodeSelector, so the app can still schedule if the labeled nodes aren’t available.
- Keep Service selectors aligned with pod labels (they are correct here: app=web-app).

I also cleaned up the short-lived test pods I created. Let me know if you want me to reintroduce a safer scheduling rule (e.g., preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution) or add node labels to match your intended topology.

results.taskOutput:
Done.

What I set up
- Namespace: multi-container-logging (verified)
- Pod: communication-pod
- Volumes: logs-volume (emptyDir) mounted at /var/log/nginx in both containers
- Containers (both in spec.containers):
  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged
    - Exposes port 8080
    - Readiness probe: HTTP GET / on port 8080 (named “http”) so the pod is Ready when the web server serves traffic
  - logger: quay.io/prometheus/busybox
    - Command: sh -c 'tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log'
- Pod securityContext: fsGroup: 101 so nginx (uid/gid 101) can write access.log on the shared volume

Current state
- Pod status: Running and Ready
- Both containers are running and the readiness probe is passing.

Optional checks
- View access log stream: kubectl -n multi-container-logging logs pod/communication-pod -c logger -f
- Generate traffic locally: kubectl -n multi-container-logging port-forward pod/communication-pod 8080:8080 and curl http://localhost:8080/ (you’ll then see entries in the logger container logs)

Steps.message:
Done.

What I set up
- Namespace: multi-container-logging (verified)
- Pod: communication-pod
- Volumes: logs-volume (emptyDir) mounted at /var/log/nginx in both containers
- Containers (both in spec.containers):
  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged
    - Exposes port 8080
    - Readiness probe: HTTP GET / on port 8080 (named “http”) so the pod is Ready when the web server serves traffic
  - logger: quay.io/prometheus/busybox
    - Command: sh -c 'tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log'
- Pod securityContext: fsGroup: 101 so nginx (uid/gid 101) can write access.log on the shared volume

Current state
- Pod status: Running and Ready
- Both containers are running and the readiness probe is passing.

Optional checks
- View access log stream: kubectl -n multi-container-logging logs pod/communication-pod -c logger -f
- Generate traffic locally: kubectl -n multi-container-logging port-forward pod/communication-pod 8080:8080 and curl http://localhost:8080/ (you’ll then see entries in the logger container logs)

  - name: my-storage
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: storage-pvc
  restartPolicy: Always
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
  schedulerName: default-scheduler
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

Done.

What I set up:
- Namespace: statefulset-test
- Headless Service: db (clusterIP: None) to back the StatefulSet
- StatefulSet: db with 3 replicas
  - Each pod mounts its own 1Gi PVC at /data (volumeClaimTemplates: data)
  - Init container writes the file /data/test with the string initial_data on first boot (if it doesn’t already exist)
  - Main container: busybox sleeping (so pods stay running)

Scaled down:
- Scaled StatefulSet db from 3 to 1
- Current pods: db-0 Running; db-1 and db-2 terminated

Verification performed:
- db-0:/data/test contains: initial_data

Notes:
- Each replica has its own PVC (data-db-0, data-db-1, data-db-2). Data persists across restarts/scales. To verify db-1 or db-2 data later, scale the StatefulSet up and exec into those pods:
  - kubectl -n statefulset-test scale sts/db --replicas=3
  - kubectl -n statefulset-test exec -it db-1 -- sh -c 'cat /data/test'
